title: Microcytic anemias
covers: Iron deficiency in depth (iron handling, hepcidin, causes, diagnosis, 2026 screening and treatment), plus thalassemia trait, anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning and sideroblastic anemia.

items.p: Small red cells mean too little hemoglobin per cell. Ask which ingredient is missing.

ul: Iron deficiency: not enough iron
Thalassemia: not enough globin
Anemia of inflammation: iron locked away by hepcidin
Lead poisoning: heme synthesis blocked
Sideroblastic anemia: iron cannot be put into heme

items.p: In children, iron deficiency and thalassemia trait are by far the most common.
Food is the only source and the body can barely excrete iron, so balance is set at the gut.

ul: Absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum: 1–2 mg a day
Vitamin C helps; phytates, tea, calcium and dairy hinder
Heme iron (meat, fish) is absorbed better than plant iron
The marrow needs about 25 mg a day; almost all of it is recycled from old red cells by macrophages
Carried on transferrin, stored as ferritin

items.p: Ferroportin is the only door by which iron leaves a cell. Hepcidin, made by the liver, locks that door.

ul: Low hepcidin (iron deficiency, anemia, hypoxia, active marrow via ERFE): more absorption and release
High hepcidin (inflammation via IL-6, iron overload): iron trapped in gut cells and macrophages; oral iron poorly absorbed

items.p: Deficiency comes before anemia: first ferritin falls, then transferrin saturation and Ret-He, and only last the hemoglobin and MCV.

ul: Low intake: breastfeeding without iron after 4–6 months; too much cow's milk (over about 700 mL a day)
Blood loss: heavy periods, gut bleeding
High demand: prematurity, growth, pregnancy
Poor absorption: celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, H. pylori, bariatric surgery

items.p: Iron deficiency in the first 3 years can harm brain development permanently, even without anemia.
Beyond pallor and fatigue: spoon nails, sore tongue, cracked mouth corners, hair loss, pica (including ice), restless legs.

ul: Ferritin: best single test. Low means deficiency. It rises with inflammation, so check CRP.
2026 thresholds: children 20 ng/mL or less; adolescents and adults 30 or less
Transferrin saturation under 20%; high RDW; low MCV; pencil cells; platelets often raised

items.p: Screen with CBC plus ferritin (not hemoglobin alone): breastfed infants at 9–12 months, formula-fed at 15–18 months, adolescent girls by age 14.

ul: Children: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once a day. Adolescents: 65 mg once a day.
Empty stomach, away from milk; vitamin C helps
Continue at least 3 months to refill stores
Reticulocytes peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises in 2–4 weeks
No response at 1 month: check adherence first, then ongoing loss, malabsorption, inflammation, wrong diagnosis
Intravenous iron: intolerance, failure of oral iron, malabsorption, heavy ongoing loss
Heavy periods: test for von Willebrand disease. Pica: test blood lead.

items.p: Confirm with hemoglobin electrophoresis. Do not give iron for microcytosis until deficiency is proven.

The second most common anemia: kidney disease, cancer, autoimmune disease, chronic infection. Normocytic at first, microcytic later; ferritin normal or high. Treat the disease; give intravenous iron if there is true deficiency (ferritin under 100 or saturation under 20%).
Children under 3 are most at risk, and iron deficiency increases lead absorption. Sources: old paint, kohl, remedies, contaminated spices.

ul: Often silent; abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, wrist or foot drop
Lead blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; zinc protoporphyrin rises
Basophilic stippling (pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase blocked); lead lines on X-ray
No safe level; reference value 3.5 µg/dL

items.note: The slide also lists ALA synthase among the enzymes inhibited by lead. Standard texts name ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

items.p: Iron enters the erythroblast but cannot be made into heme. Ferritin and saturation are high; the marrow shows ring sideroblasts (Prussian blue).

ul: Inherited: X-linked ALAS2 (responds to vitamin B6)
Acquired: isoniazid, linezolid, alcohol, lead, myelodysplasia, copper deficiency, zinc excess

cards.a: Iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of inflammation (late), lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia

cards.q: Where is iron absorbed, and what helps or hinders?
cards.a: Duodenum and proximal jejunum; vitamin C helps; phytates, tea, calcium, dairy hinder
Binds ferroportin and causes its destruction, trapping iron in gut cells and macrophages

cards.q: What lowers and what raises hepcidin?
cards.a: Lowers: iron deficiency, hypoxia, ERFE. Raises: inflammation (IL-6), iron overload.
Iron depletion (low ferritin), iron-deficient erythropoiesis (low TSAT, low Ret-He), iron deficiency anemia
Absolute: body iron too low. Functional: iron present but locked in stores (inflammation, kidney disease).

cards.q: Ferritin in iron deficiency versus anemia of inflammation
cards.a: Low versus normal or high (transferrin saturation is low in both)
Koilonychia, glossitis, angular stomatitis, hair loss, pica and pagophagia, restless legs

cards.q: Milk and iron deficiency: the limits
cards.a: No cow's milk before 12 months; no more than about 24 oz (700 mL) a day afterwards
CBC + ferritin (with CRP): breastfed at 9–12 months, formula-fed at 15–18 months, adolescents by age 14
Children 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily; adolescents 65 mg once daily; at least 3 months
Reticulocyte peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises in 2–4 weeks; stores refilled after 3 months

cards.q: Most common cause of failure of oral iron
cards.a: Non-adherence or underdosing
Oral intolerance, no response, malabsorption (IBD, celiac, bariatric surgery), ongoing losses
Hypophosphatemia
Trait: high RBC count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer < 13. Iron deficiency: the opposite.
Normocytic then microcytic, low reticulocytes, low TSAT, normal or high ferritin, high hepcidin
ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase (zinc protoporphyrin rises)

cards.q: Why basophilic stippling in lead poisoning?
cards.a: Lead inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA clumps.
Abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, wrist or foot drop, lead lines on X-ray

cards.q: Sideroblastic anemia: hallmark and iron tests
cards.a: Ring sideroblasts in marrow; high ferritin and transferrin saturation
X-linked ALAS2 mutation; also give B6 with isoniazid-related cases

cards.q: Adolescent with iron deficiency and heavy periods: screen for...
cards.a: von Willebrand disease

cards.q: Toddler with iron deficiency and pica: test...
cards.a: Blood lead level

questions.stem: Each microcytic anemia lacks one ingredient of hemoglobin. Which pairing is correct?

options.A: Sideroblastic anemia: iron not inserted into heme
options.B: Sideroblastic anemia: not enough globin
options.C: Thalassemia: iron locked away by hepcidin
options.D: Anemia of inflammation: heme synthesis blocked
options.E: Lead poisoning: not enough iron

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency: not enough iron. Thalassemia: too little globin. Anemia of inflammation: iron locked away by hepcidin. Lead poisoning: heme synthesis blocked. Sideroblastic anemia: iron not inserted into heme. B: That is thalassemia. C: That is anemia of inflammation. D: That is lead poisoning. E: That is iron deficiency.

questions.stem: Which microcytic anemias dominate in children, and which is more common in adults?

options.A: Anemia of inflammation and lead poisoning dominate in children; iron deficiency in adults
options.B: Sideroblastic anemia dominates in children; thalassemia trait in adults
options.C: Thalassemia trait dominates at each age
options.D: Iron deficiency and thalassemia trait dominate in children; inflammation in adults
options.E: Iron deficiency and lead poisoning dominate in children; sideroblastic anemia in adults

questions.explanation: In children, iron deficiency and thalassemia trait dominate; anemia of inflammation is more common in adults. A: Not as stated. B: Not as stated. C: Not as stated. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: How common is iron deficiency in US toddlers, and why does it matter beyond anemia?

options.A: About 15%; cognitive deficits resolve fully once hemoglobin is normal
options.B: About 1.5%; cognitive deficits may persist after correction
options.C: About 50%; growth is affected but cognition is spared
options.D: About 15%; the main risk is iron overload from treatment
options.E: About 15%; cognitive deficits may persist after correction

questions.explanation: About 15% of US toddlers and about 11% of non-pregnant adolescent girls have iron deficiency. It is linked to neurodevelopmental and cognitive deficits that may persist even after anemia is corrected. A: Deficits may persist. B: The figure is about 15%. C: Not the data given. D: Not the concern stated.

questions.stem: Put the stages of iron deficiency in order and match the first abnormal test of each stage.

options.A: Iron depletion: low TSAT; iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low ferritin; anemia: low Hb
options.B: Iron depletion: low ferritin; iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low TSAT; anemia: low Hb
options.C: Iron depletion: low Hb; iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low MCV; anemia: low ferritin
options.D: Iron depletion: high RDW; iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low ferritin; anemia: low TSAT
options.E: Iron depletion: low ferritin; iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low Hb; anemia: low TSAT

questions.explanation: Stage 1 iron depletion: stores fall, ferritin low, Hb/MCV/MCH normal. Stage 2 iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low TSAT, low Ret-He, high ZPP, Hb still normal. Stage 3 iron deficiency anemia: Hb falls, microcytosis, hypochromia, high RDW. A: Ferritin falls first. C: Hb falls last. D: RDW rises in stage 3. E: Hb is still normal in stage 2.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has adequate total body iron, but circulating iron is low because it is locked in stores. Which term applies?

options.A: Absolute iron deficiency
options.B: Iron depletion
options.C: Functional iron deficiency
options.D: Iron-refractory iron deficiency anemia
options.E: Sideroblastic anemia

questions.explanation: Absolute iron deficiency: total body iron too low (poor intake, blood loss, malabsorption, rapid growth). Functional iron deficiency: iron adequate but locked in stores (inflammation, chronic kidney disease, high hepcidin). A: Total body iron would be too low. B: That is stage 1 of absolute deficiency. D: That is a rare inherited disorder. E: Iron is not inserted into heme there.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a listed role of iron EXCEPT:

options.A: Oxygen delivery to muscle by myoglobin
options.B: ATP generation by mitochondrial enzymes
options.C: Myelination and neurotransmitters
options.D: Synthesis of DNA bases
options.E: Normal immune function

questions.explanation: Iron is needed for hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial enzymes (ATP), immunity and brain growth (myelination, neurotransmitters). A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about dietary iron is correct?

options.A: Non-heme iron from plants is more bioavailable than heme iron
options.B: Heme iron comes from fortified cereals and legumes
options.C: Heme iron from meat and fish is more bioavailable
options.D: Heme and non-heme iron are absorbed equally
options.E: Non-heme iron is found in meat, poultry and fish

questions.explanation: Heme iron (meat, poultry, fish) has higher bioavailability; non-heme iron (plants, cereals, legumes, fortified foods) lower. A: Reversed. B: Those supply non-heme iron. D: Heme iron is absorbed more easily. E: Those supply heme iron.

questions.stem: Where is iron mainly absorbed, and what changes absorption?

options.A: Duodenum and proximal jejunum; vitamin C raises it, phytates lower it
options.B: Terminal ileum; vitamin C increases it, phytates and dairy reduce it
options.C: Duodenum and proximal jejunum; calcium increases it, vitamin C reduces it
options.D: Stomach; tea increases it, vitamin C reduces it
options.E: Colon; phytates increase it, dairy reduces it

questions.explanation: Absorption is mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Vitamin C increases it; phytates, tea, calcium and dairy reduce it. B: The site is duodenum and proximal jejunum. C: Reversed. D: Not as stated. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: During which period may the effects of iron deficiency on the brain be irreversible, even without anemia?

options.A: 5–10 years
options.B: Adolescence
options.C: After 36 months
options.D: In utero exclusively
options.E: 0–36 months

questions.explanation: Effects of deficiency at 0–36 months may be irreversible, even without anemia. Iron deficiency also causes more severe infections (reduced bactericidal activity of macrophages). A: Not the window given. B: Not the window given. C: The window is 0–36 months. D: Not the window given.

questions.stem: Which figures describe daily iron traffic?

options.A: Gut absorbs about 25 mg; marrow uses 1–2 mg; macrophages recycle 1–2 mg
options.B: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg; marrow uses 25 mg; macrophages recycle 25 mg
options.C: Gut absorbs 1–2 g; marrow uses about 25 g; macrophages recycle about 25 g
options.D: Gut absorbs 3–4 mg; marrow uses about 2 g; macrophages recycle 1–2 mg
options.E: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg; marrow uses about 25 mg; kidneys excrete about 25 mg

questions.explanation: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg/day; transferrin carries only 3–4 mg at a time; marrow uses about 25 mg/day; red cells hold about 2 g; spleen macrophages recycle about 25 mg/day. Total body iron 3–4 g. A: Reversed. C: The units are milligrams. D: Not the figures given. E: The body has very limited excretion.

questions.stem: Why is the gut the control point of iron balance?

options.A: The kidneys excrete excess iron when ferritin is high
options.B: The liver destroys excess iron
options.C: Iron is lost freely in bile
options.D: Macrophages cannot release iron
options.E: The body recycles iron but has very limited excretion

questions.explanation: The body recycles iron but has very limited excretion; balance is set at the gut by hepcidin. Daily losses of 1–2 mg are replaced by absorbing the same amount. A: There is very limited excretion. B: Not a mechanism. C: Not as stated. D: They recycle about 25 mg/day.

questions.stem: Which cell is matched with its role in iron handling?

options.A: Erythroblast: exports iron through ferroportin
options.B: Hepatocyte: absorbs iron from food
options.C: Enterocyte: senses iron and makes hepcidin
options.D: Erythroblast: transferrin receptor 1 uptake
options.E: Macrophage: makes erythroferrone

questions.explanation: Enterocyte absorbs iron and releases it through ferroportin; hepatocyte stores iron and makes hepcidin; macrophage recycles iron from old red cells and releases it through ferroportin; erythroblast takes iron in through transferrin receptor 1. A: Enterocytes and macrophages export through ferroportin. B: That is the enterocyte. C: That is the hepatocyte. E: ERFE comes from red cell precursors.

questions.stem: What happens when hepcidin is high?

options.A: Ferroportin stays on the surface, releasing iron from gut cells and macrophages
options.B: Transferrin receptor 1 is destroyed, trapping iron in plasma
options.C: Ferroportin is internalized and destroyed, trapping iron in cells
options.D: Ferritin is degraded, releasing iron into blood
options.E: Ferroportin is up-regulated in the liver, raising blood iron

questions.explanation: Hepcidin binds ferroportin, the only door for iron to leave a cell; ferroportin is pulled in and destroyed, iron is trapped inside gut cells and macrophages, and blood iron falls. A: That is low hepcidin. B: Hepcidin acts on ferroportin. D: Not the mechanism. E: Blood iron falls.

questions.stem: Which signals lower hepcidin?

options.A: Iron overload, inflammation and IL-6
options.B: Iron deficiency, hypoxia and ERFE
options.C: Iron deficiency, infection and IL-6
options.D: Hypoxia, iron overload and ERFE
options.E: Inflammation, anemia and ERFE

questions.explanation: Hepcidin goes down with iron deficiency, anemia and hypoxia, and busy red cell production (erythroblasts send ERFE). It goes up with iron overload and inflammation/infection (IL-6). A: These raise hepcidin. C: Infection and IL-6 raise it. D: Iron overload raises it. E: Inflammation raises it.

questions.stem: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis takes oral iron without benefit. Which mediator explains the poor absorption?

options.A: IL-6 raising hepcidin
options.B: ERFE lowering hepcidin
options.C: Erythropoietin raising ferroportin
options.D: Vitamin C lowering hepcidin
options.E: IL-5 raising transferrin

questions.explanation: Inflammation and infection (IL-6) raise hepcidin: the door locks, iron is trapped in stores, blood iron falls, and oral iron is poorly absorbed. B: That would increase absorption. C: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which test distinguishes iron deficiency anemia from anemia of inflammation?

options.A: TSAT tells them apart; ferritin is low in both
options.B: MCV tells them apart; ferritin is high in both
options.C: Serum iron tells them apart; TSAT is high in both
options.D: Reticulocyte count tells them apart; ferritin is normal in both
options.E: Ferritin tells them apart; TSAT is low in both

questions.explanation: Both have low blood iron and low TSAT. Iron deficiency: low hepcidin, empty stores, low ferritin, oral iron absorbed well. Anemia of inflammation: high hepcidin, stores full but locked, ferritin normal or high, oral iron poorly absorbed. A: Reversed. B: Not as stated. C: Blood iron is low in both. D: Not as stated.

questions.stem: Which cause of iron deficiency acts by decreasing absorption?

options.A: Heavy menstrual bleeding
options.B: Prematurity
options.C: Bariatric surgery
options.D: Excess cow's milk
options.E: Frequent blood sampling

questions.explanation: Decreased absorption: celiac disease, IBD, atrophic gastritis, H. pylori, bariatric surgery, rarely IRIDA. Decreased intake: exclusive breastfeeding without iron after 4–6 months, excess cow's milk. Blood loss: heavy menses, GI loss, frequent sampling. Increased demand: growth, pregnancy, prematurity. A: Blood loss. B: Increased demand. D: Decreased intake. E: Blood loss.

questions.stem: Above which daily volume does milk intake put a toddler at high risk of iron deficiency (AAP 2026)?

options.A: More than 8 oz (about 240 mL)
options.B: More than 24 oz (about 700 mL)
options.C: More than 12 oz (about 350 mL)
options.D: More than 40 oz (about 1200 mL)
options.E: Any cow's milk after 12 months

questions.explanation: High risk: cow's milk before 12 months, or more than 24 oz (about 700 mL) a day of cow's or plant milk; also preterm infants, exclusively breastfed infants without iron after 4–6 months, menstruating adolescents, low-iron diets, pregnancy. A: The limit given is 24 oz. C: The limit given is 24 oz. D: The limit given is 24 oz. E: Cow's milk is allowed after 12 months within the limit.

questions.stem: Which findings come from iron deficiency itself and not from the anemia?

options.A: Pallor, palpitations and shortness of breath
options.B: Angina and heart failure
options.C: Jaundice and dark urine
options.D: Koilonychia, pagophagia and restless legs
options.E: Easy fatigability and pallor

questions.explanation: From iron deficiency itself: glossitis, angular stomatitis, koilonychia (spoon nails), hair loss, pica including pagophagia (ice), poor memory, restless legs. Many appear before anemia. A: These are from the anemia. B: These are from severe anemia. C: Not features of iron deficiency. E: These are from the anemia.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern suggests iron deficiency?

options.A: TSAT below 20%, raised soluble transferrin receptor, high RDW
options.B: TSAT above 45%, low soluble transferrin receptor, RDW above 16%
options.C: TSAT below 20%, low soluble transferrin receptor, normal RDW
options.D: High ferritin, high TSAT, ring sideroblasts
options.E: Normal ferritin, normal RDW, high red cell count

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, TSAT <20%, raised soluble transferrin receptor, low MCV and MCH, RDW high (>16%), low Ret-He (also low in thalassemia trait). B: TSAT is low and sTfR raised. C: sTfR is raised and RDW high. D: That is sideroblastic anemia. E: That suggests thalassemia trait.

questions.stem: What is typical on the blood smear and platelet count in iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: Microcytic hypochromic cells and target cells; platelets often low
options.B: Macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; platelets normal
options.C: Spherocytes and polychromasia; platelets normal
options.D: Basophilic stippling and schistocytes; platelets low
options.E: Microcytic hypochromic cells and pencil forms; platelets often raised

questions.explanation: Smear: microcytic, hypochromic cells, pencil forms; platelets often raised. A: Platelets are often raised, and pencil forms are typical. B: That is megaloblastic anemia. C: That suggests hemolysis. D: Not iron deficiency.

questions.stem: Why can a normal ferritin fail to exclude iron deficiency, and what should be checked with it?

options.A: Ferritin falls with inflammation; check TSAT
options.B: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; check CRP
options.C: Ferritin varies with meals; draw it fasting
options.D: Ferritin reflects iron supply, not stores; check Ret-He
options.E: Ferritin is unreliable in children; check hemoglobin instead

questions.explanation: Ferritin is the best single marker of total body iron, but it is an acute-phase reactant: a normal value cannot exclude deficiency during inflammation. Check CRP with ferritin. A: Ferritin rises with inflammation. C: Fasting applies to TSAT. D: Ferritin reflects stores. E: Hemoglobin by itself is no longer advised.

questions.stem: How should blood for transferrin saturation be drawn?

options.A: After a meal rich in iron
options.B: After an oral iron dose, to test absorption
options.C: At any time; TSAT does not vary
options.D: Fasting, without iron beforehand
options.E: Together with vitamin C

questions.explanation: TSAT reflects iron available for red cell production; draw fasting and avoid iron or multivitamins beforehand. A: It should be fasting. B: Iron should be avoided beforehand. C: Fasting is advised. E: Not advised.

questions.stem: Which ferritin values suggest iron deficiency under the 2026 thresholds?

options.A: Children ≤ 12 ng/mL; adults with inflammation < 30 ng/mL
options.B: Children ≤ 30 ng/mL; adults with inflammation < 50 ng/mL
options.C: Children ≤ 20 ng/mL; adults with inflammation < 100 ng/mL
options.D: Children ≤ 20 ng/mL; adults with inflammation < 20 ng/mL
options.E: Children ≤ 50 ng/mL; adults with inflammation < 200 ng/mL

questions.explanation: Children ≤20 ng/mL; adolescents and adults ≤30 (up to ≤50 with symptoms or risk factors). With inflammation in adults: ferritin <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20%. A: These are older or other values. B: Not the thresholds. D: With inflammation the cutoff is <100. E: Not the thresholds.

questions.stem: When does AAP 2026 advise screening for iron deficiency?

options.A: Breastfed infants at 9–12 months; adolescents by age 14
options.B: Breastfed infants at 15–18 months; adolescents at menarche
options.C: Each infant at 12 months by hemoglobin; no adolescent screening
options.D: Breastfed infants at 9–12 months; adolescents after age 18
options.E: Preterm infants at 2 weeks; adolescents yearly from age 10

questions.explanation: Screen breastfed infants at 9–12 months; formula-fed infants at 15–18 months after the switch to cow's or plant milk; children with risk factors yearly to age 4; adolescents with CBC + ferritin ≥1 year after menarche or by age 14, yearly if heavy bleeding. B: 15–18 months is for formula-fed infants. C: That is the replaced 2010 approach. D: Screening is by age 14. E: Preterm infants start iron by 2 weeks; that is not screening.

questions.stem: Which tests does AAP 2026 use for screening?

options.A: Hemoglobin by itself at 12 months
options.B: CBC and ferritin with CRP
options.C: Ferritin by itself without a CBC
options.D: TSAT and soluble transferrin receptor
options.E: CBC and blood lead in each child

questions.explanation: Test CBC and ferritin (not Hb alone) and add CRP, because inflammation makes ferritin falsely reassuring. This replaces the 2010 report and Hb-only screening at 12 months. A: That is the replaced approach. C: CBC and ferritin are both used. D: Not the screening tests. E: Lead is tested with iron deficiency or pica.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is matched with the right group?

options.A: Exclusively breastfed infants: iron 3 mg/kg/day from birth
options.B: Preterm infants: iron 1 mg/kg/day from 6 months
options.C: Term newborns: immediate cord clamping
options.D: Exclusively breastfed infants: iron 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months
options.E: Toddlers: cow's milk from 6 months, unlimited

questions.explanation: Prevention: delayed cord clamping; preterm infants 2–3 mg/kg/day by 2 weeks; exclusively breastfed infants 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months; no cow's milk before 1 year and limit to about 24 oz a day; iron-rich foods; iron for pregnant women. A: The dose is 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months. B: Preterm infants get 2–3 mg/kg/day by 2 weeks. C: Delayed cord clamping is advised. E: No cow's milk before 1 year; limit to about 24 oz.

questions.stem: What oral iron regimen does AAP 2026 give for iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: 6 mg/kg elemental iron three times daily in children; 65 mg twice daily in adolescents
options.B: 1 mg/kg elemental iron once daily in children; 325 mg once daily in adolescents
options.C: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily in children; 65 mg once daily in adolescents
options.D: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once weekly in children; 65 mg once weekly in adolescents
options.E: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily for 2 weeks at each age

questions.explanation: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily for children (usually ferrous sulfate); 65 mg elemental iron once daily for adolescents; at least 3 months, then recheck ferritin and extend 3 months if still <20 ng/mL. A: Dosing is once daily at 3 mg/kg. B: 1 mg/kg is a preventive dose; 325 mg is the ferrous sulfate salt. D: Dosing is daily. E: Treatment lasts at least 3 months.

questions.stem: How should oral iron be taken, and what should families be warned about?

options.A: With milk to protect the stomach; dark stools and tooth staining
options.B: With tea or calcium; constipation exclusively
options.C: On an empty stomach, away from vitamin C; red urine
options.D: With meals rich in phytates; no warnings needed
options.E: On an empty stomach, away from milk; dark stools and tooth staining

questions.explanation: Give on an empty stomach, away from milk and dairy; vitamin C helps. Warn about dark stools and tooth staining. Every-other-day dosing may be better tolerated (AGA 2024). A: Milk reduces absorption. B: These reduce absorption. C: Vitamin C helps. D: Phytates reduce absorption.

questions.stem: A toddler with iron deficiency has Hb 6.5 g/dL and is clinically stable. How should she be managed?

options.A: Oral iron with close follow-up
options.B: Immediate rapid transfusion
options.C: Intravenous iron as first line
options.D: Observation without iron until ferritin returns
options.E: Slow transfusion in small aliquots

questions.explanation: Severe anemia (Hb ≤7 g/dL): clinically stable, oral iron with close follow-up; unstable, slow transfusion in small aliquots. Follow up at 1 and 3 months. B: Transfusion is for unstable patients, slowly in small aliquots. C: In children IV iron is for specialist referral in specific indications. D: Treatment is indicated. E: That is for unstable patients.

questions.stem: What is the expected timeline of response to oral iron?

options.A: Reticulocyte peak at 2–4 weeks; hemoglobin rises at days 5–10; stores refilled after 3 months
options.B: Reticulocyte peak at days 1–3; hemoglobin normal at 1 week; stores refilled at 1 month
options.C: Reticulocyte peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises at 2–4 weeks; stores refilled after 3 months
options.D: Reticulocyte peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises at 3 months; stores refilled after 1 year
options.E: Hemoglobin rises at days 1–3; reticulocytes fall at 2–4 weeks

questions.explanation: Days 1–3: feels better. Days 5–10: reticulocyte peak. 2–4 weeks: Hb rises (at 1 month, normal Hb in mild anemia or a rise ≥2 g/dL in severe anemia). ≥3 months: stores refilled, ferritin normalizes. A: The first two are swapped. B: Too fast. D: Too slow. E: Not the timeline.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin has not risen after 1 month of oral iron. What should be checked first?

options.A: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.B: Dose and adherence
options.C: Endoscopy for celiac disease
options.D: TMPRSS6 sequencing
options.E: Bone marrow aspirate

questions.explanation: No rise in Hb after 1 month: check the dose and adherence first (non-adherence or underdosing is the most common cause), then ongoing loss, malabsorption, inflammation or another diagnosis. A: Wrong diagnosis is considered after adherence. C: Malabsorption is considered after adherence. D: IRIDA is rare. E: Not the first step.

questions.stem: Each of the following is an indication for intravenous iron EXCEPT:

options.A: Intolerance of oral iron
options.B: No response to an adequate oral trial
options.C: Celiac disease or bariatric surgery blocking absorption
options.D: Ongoing losses that oral iron cannot match
options.E: Mild anemia in a patient who has not yet tried oral iron

questions.explanation: IV iron: oral intolerance, no response to an adequate trial, conditions blocking absorption (IBD, celiac disease, bariatric surgery), ongoing losses. Children are referred to a specialist. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: Which practical point about intravenous iron is correct?

options.A: Ferric carboxymaltose can cause hyperkalemia
options.B: Most reactions are true anaphylaxis
options.C: Products needing many small infusions are preferred
options.D: Ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphatemia
options.E: Newer oral formulations outperform ferrous sulfate

questions.explanation: Prefer products that replace the deficit in 1–2 infusions; most reactions are infusion reactions, not true anaphylaxis; ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphatemia (check phosphate with repeated doses); no oral formulation beats ferrous sulfate, which is the cheapest. A: The risk named is hypophosphatemia. B: Most are infusion reactions. C: Prefer replacement in 1–2 infusions. E: No oral formulation beats ferrous sulfate.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with heavy menstrual flow has Hb 9 g/dL and MCV 70 fL. Besides confirming iron deficiency with ferritin and CRP, which condition should be screened for?

options.A: von Willebrand disease
options.B: Celiac disease of the gut
options.C: Lead poisoning
options.D: Thalassemia trait
options.E: Hemophilia A

questions.explanation: Case 1: iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding; screen for von Willebrand disease; confirm ferritin <30 ng/mL with CRP; treat with 65 mg elemental iron daily and manage the bleeding. B: A cause of malabsorption, not suggested by heavy bleeding. C: Suggested by pica in toddlers. D: Not suggested by the bleeding history. E: The lecture names von Willebrand disease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old on large amounts of cow's milk craves ice, soil and paper. Hb is 8.0 g/dL and MCV 65 fL. What else should be tested, and why?

options.A: Vitamin B12; pica causes malabsorption
options.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis; pica suggests thalassemia
options.C: Stool parasites; soil eating causes hemolysis
options.D: Copper; pica causes sideroblastic anemia
options.E: Blood lead; it often coexists with iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Case 2: nutritional iron deficiency anemia. Pica (soil, paper): check a blood lead level, because lead and iron deficiency often coexist. Treat with 3 mg/kg/day elemental iron, limit milk, iron-rich foods; recheck at 1 and 3 months. A: Not the reasoning given. B: Not the reasoning given. C: Not the reasoning given. D: Not the reasoning given.

questions.stem: Which profile points to thalassemia trait and not iron deficiency?

options.A: Low red cell count, high RDW, low ferritin, Mentzer index above 13
options.B: High red cell count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer index below 13
options.C: High red cell count, high RDW, low ferritin, Mentzer index below 13
options.D: Low red cell count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer index above 13
options.E: Normal red cell count, high RDW, high ferritin, ring sideroblasts

questions.explanation: Thalassemia trait: high RBC count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) <13. Iron deficiency: low RBC count, high RDW, low ferritin, Mentzer >13. Confirm with Hb electrophoresis or HPLC. A: That is iron deficiency. C: RDW and ferritin are normal in trait. D: Red cell count is high and the index low in trait. E: That suggests sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: What rule does the lecture give about iron for microcytosis?

options.A: Give a trial of iron to each microcytic child
options.B: Give iron if the Mentzer index is below 13
options.C: Give iron if the red cell count is high
options.D: No iron without confirming deficiency
options.E: Give iron until electrophoresis is available

questions.explanation: Never give iron for microcytosis without confirming iron deficiency; thalassemia is the key mimic. A: Thalassemia trait is a mimic. B: That suggests trait. C: That suggests trait. E: Confirm deficiency first.

questions.stem: Which new thalassemia treatment is matched with its nature?

options.A: Mitapivat: CRISPR gene editing; exa-cel: oral pyruvate kinase activator
options.B: Luspatercept: oral iron chelator; mitapivat: erythroid maturation agent
options.C: Mitapivat: oral pyruvate kinase activator; exa-cel: CRISPR gene editing
options.D: Exa-cel: erythroid maturation agent; luspatercept: gene editing
options.E: Mitapivat: hepcidin mimetic; exa-cel: stem cell donor graft

questions.explanation: Exa-cel (Casgevy, FDA Jan 2024): CRISPR gene editing for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, age ≥12, about 9 in 10 transfusion-independent. Mitapivat (FDA Dec 2025): first oral drug, a pyruvate kinase activator. Luspatercept: erythroid maturation agent. A: Reversed. B: Luspatercept is the erythroid maturation agent. D: Reversed. E: Not their nature.

questions.stem: Which statement about anemia of inflammation is correct?

options.A: Second most common anemia; normocytic early, then microcytic
options.B: The most common anemia; microcytic early, normocytic late
options.C: The second most common anemia; macrocytic throughout
options.D: A rare anemia; high reticulocytes and low ferritin
options.E: The second most common anemia; low hepcidin and empty stores

questions.explanation: Anemia of inflammation is the #2 most common anemia. Causes: CKD, cancer, autoimmune disease, chronic infection or inflammation. High hepcidin traps iron in macrophages; less EPO and a blunted marrow response; normocytic early, microcytic late; low reticulocytes; low–normal TSAT; normal or high ferritin. B: It is second after iron deficiency, and normocytic early. C: Not macrocytic. D: Reticulocytes are low and ferritin normal or high. E: Hepcidin is high and stores full.

questions.stem: How is anemia of inflammation managed?

options.A: Oral iron for 3 months in each patient
options.B: Transfusion as first line, then chelation
options.C: ESAs in each patient; iron is contraindicated
options.D: Treat the disease; IV iron if deficient
options.E: Pyridoxine and removal of offending drugs

questions.explanation: Treat the underlying disease; look for coexisting iron deficiency (ferritin <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20%); IV iron if deficient; ESAs in selected cases (e.g. CKD). A: Oral iron is poorly absorbed with high hepcidin. B: Not the approach. C: ESAs are for selected cases, and coexisting deficiency is treated. E: That is for sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a listed source of lead EXCEPT:

options.A: Kohl
options.B: Old paint and dust
options.C: Cow's milk
options.D: Traditional remedies
options.E: Contaminated spices

questions.explanation: Sources: old lead-based paint and dust, kohl, traditional remedies, industry, auto-repair work, contaminated spices and foods. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Why are children under 3 most vulnerable to lead, and how does iron status matter?

options.A: Low gastric acid and a mature blood–brain barrier; iron deficiency reduces lead absorption
options.B: Hand-to-mouth activity, immature blood–brain barrier; iron deficiency increases lead absorption
options.C: Higher lead excretion; iron overload increases lead absorption
options.D: Hand-to-mouth activity; iron status has no effect
options.E: Breastfeeding; iron supplements carry lead

questions.explanation: Children under 3: more hand-to-mouth activity, immature blood–brain barrier, and iron deficiency increases lead absorption. A: Reversed on both counts. C: Not as stated. D: Iron deficiency increases absorption. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old living in an old house has abdominal pain, constipation, irritability and developmental delay. Which additional sign of high lead levels does the lecture list?

options.A: Wrist and foot drop
options.B: Spoon-shaped nails
options.C: Splenomegaly
options.D: Jaundice
options.E: Petechiae

questions.explanation: Lead poisoning is often silent; features include abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, encephalopathy at high levels, and wrist and foot drop. Effects are often irreversible. B: A sign of iron deficiency. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which findings support the diagnosis of lead poisoning?

options.A: Ring sideroblasts, high ferritin and high TSAT
options.B: Pencil cells, low ferritin and high platelets
options.C: Target cells, high red cell count and normal RDW
options.D: Spherocytes, high reticulocytes and jaundice
options.E: Basophilic stippling, high ZPP and lead lines

questions.explanation: Diagnosis: microcytic anemia, low reticulocytes, coarse basophilic stippling, high blood lead and ZPP; dense metaphyseal lead lines on X-ray. A: That is sideroblastic anemia. B: That is iron deficiency. C: That is thalassemia trait. D: That suggests hemolysis.

questions.stem: What is the CDC blood lead reference value, and who should be tested?

options.A: 3.5 µg/dL; children with iron deficiency or pica
options.B: 10 µg/dL; children with encephalopathy
options.C: 3.5 µg/dL; adults with occupational exposure exclusively
options.D: 35 µg/dL; children with pica
options.E: 0.35 µg/dL; each child yearly

questions.explanation: There is no safe blood lead level. CDC reference value: 3.5 µg/dL. Test children with iron deficiency or pica. B: The reference value is 3.5, and testing is broader. C: Children with iron deficiency or pica are tested. D: The value is 3.5. E: The value is 3.5.

questions.stem: Which enzymes of heme synthesis does lead inhibit?

options.A: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase and ferrochelatase
options.B: Porphobilinogen deaminase and ALA dehydratase
options.C: Heme oxygenase and biliverdin reductase
options.D: ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
options.E: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase and heme oxygenase

questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase (the slide also lists ALA synthase); ALA accumulates, iron cannot be inserted, so zinc is: zinc protoporphyrin rises (iron deficiency raises it too). A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: These degrade heme. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: What causes basophilic stippling in lead poisoning?

options.A: Inhibition of ferrochelatase, so iron aggregates in mitochondria
options.B: Inhibition of pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase; RNA aggregates
options.C: Precipitation of denatured hemoglobin
options.D: Retained nuclear fragments
options.E: Inhibition of ALA dehydratase, so ALA aggregates

questions.explanation: Lead inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA aggregates in red cells; it also causes oxidative stress. A: That would give ring sideroblasts. C: Those are Heinz bodies. D: Not the mechanism given. E: Not the mechanism of stippling.

questions.stem: What was the source of the 2023–2024 US lead outbreak described in the lecture?

options.A: Kohl imported for infants
options.B: Old paint in day-care centres
options.C: Cinnamon applesauce pouches
options.D: Powdered infant formula
options.E: Municipal water pipes

questions.explanation: 566 cases were linked to cinnamon applesauce pouches (cinnamon adulterated with lead chromate, food fraud); 96% were children under 6. FDA action levels for lead in baby food are 10–20 ppb (Jan 2025). A: Not the source of that outbreak. B: Not the source of that outbreak. D: Not the source of that outbreak. E: Not the source of that outbreak.

questions.stem: Which inherited form of sideroblastic anemia responds to pyridoxine?

options.A: Autosomal recessive SLC25A38 mutations
options.B: TMPRSS6 mutations
options.C: LYST mutations
options.D: Ferrochelatase mutations
options.E: X-linked ALAS2 mutations

questions.explanation: Inherited: X-linked ALAS2 mutations (milder, pyridoxine-responsive) and autosomal recessive SLC25A38 (severe, transfusion-dependent). A: Severe and transfusion-dependent. B: That is IRIDA. C: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: Not listed.

questions.stem: A patient treated for tuberculosis develops microcytic anemia with high ferritin and high TSAT. Which drug is a listed cause, and which other acquired causes are named?

options.A: Rifampin; also copper excess and zinc deficiency
options.B: Isoniazid; also copper deficiency and zinc excess
options.C: Isoniazid; also iron deficiency and thalassemia
options.D: Ethambutol; also B12 deficiency
options.E: Pyrazinamide; also lead and aspirin

questions.explanation: Acquired sideroblastic anemia: drugs and toxins (isoniazid, linezolid, alcohol, lead), myelodysplastic syndrome, copper deficiency, zinc excess. A: The metal imbalances are reversed and rifampin is not listed. C: Those are separate microcytic anemias. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: What defines sideroblastic anemia on bone marrow examination, and how is it treated?

options.A: Ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue; give oral iron
options.B: Basophilic stippling on Wright stain; chelation of lead
options.C: Megaloblasts; give B12 and folate
options.D: Ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue; give pyridoxine
options.E: Absent iron stores; give IV iron

questions.explanation: High ferritin and TSAT; ring sideroblasts (erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria around the nucleus, Prussian blue). Remove the offending agent, give pyridoxine, treat the cause; transfusion and chelation when needed. A: Iron is already high. B: That is lead poisoning. C: That is megaloblastic anemia. E: Ferritin and TSAT are high.
